speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
My very short experience
in politics has not led me to believe that a board given full control, such as the present trustees, is so vastly more impregnable to political influence than a board that has contact through a responsible minister. The minister has no powers in connection with the board of directors that he has not under the other board. The minister has no power to do with the railway as he likes. Large matters, matters of importance, arise almost every week wdiich necessitate discussion between someone in authority in the railway and someone in authority in the government. For instance the government is still the trustee of a great deal of railway property that is operated as part of the Canadian National system, and the Canadian National Railways are operating steamships which the government owns. Matters of that kind require conferences between the two bodies. These conferences are held between the responsible minister and the chairman of the board or someone who has the authority to represent the railway. That is the only connection that is provided between the government and the board of management. In other days we used to have a representative
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

of the minister on the board. That has been changed, for just the reason my hon. friend suggests, that such connection might be used to influence the board in respect of matters on which the government should have no say, matters purely relative to the railway. All that is done away with. But as regards matters concerning which the government must confer with the railway and the railway with the government there is provision for such conferences between the head of the railway and the head of the department at Ottawa, that is, between the Minister of Railways and the chairman of the board. I think that is the only proper contact, and as such it is provided for.
How my hon. friend can say that this is going to lead to graft and corruption on a scale never before known in Canada I cannot understand. It is assuming that you have a very corrupt minister of railways and a very corrupt chairman of the board of directors. It must be so, because these two provide the only contact between the railway and the government. They must both be corrupt and not one alone, if graft and corruption are to exist. It seems to me that my hon. friend used rather strong language in that connection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I trust the minister has all the virtues. Undoubtedly his past life discloses that he is a man of high character and very considerable experience, but he has never been subjected to the political influences emanating from 170 or 180 members of parliament, each of whom is anxious to obtain some advantage for his constituency. The other day the minister professed that he did not understand very much about the exercise of political influence upon governments and ministers in the administration of public properties, but I suggest to him that whdn two years hence he comes back to meet us his eyes will have been opened, and he will know something more about practical politics as accepted in the public life of Canada.
In one respect I cannot see very much change. It is true that instead of trustees we are to have a board of governors. This board is not to give its whole time to the administration; one director of the national company is appointed chairman of the board of directors. I assume he would be chairman of the board of directors of the national company. It was suggested that Mr. Fullerton, as chairman, had certain veto powers, but this gentleman who is to be appointed chairman has practically all the powers of the board. He will be there all the time. He
[Mr. Howe.l
will be on the job, and the others will not be on the job a sufficient length of time to find out what is being done, or to advise as to how it should be done.
But that is not the point I wished to make when I said the bill opened the way to political influence. In 1933, after comparatively slight criticism, a bill was passed by a very large majority, and was passed unanimously in another place. That measure solemnly declared that for a certain length of time the board of trustees should be constituted and, except under certain prescribed methods, parliament relieved itself of the responsibility of changing that board. The present bill is a complete repudiation of what parliament did in 1933. It is a violation of the solemn pledge of parliament to these men to the effect that in their appointment as trustees they would 'be retained for a certain length of time without interference. It is a repudiation of the very platform upon which they were appointed, whereby they were to be relieved completely from political pressure, placed in a position where they would be above political influence and capable of administering the railways in the interests of all the people of Canada without fear or favour of any political party. The present measure repudiates that pledge. It starts out by saying that we are to repeal the act of 1933 in so far as it appointed these trustees to act as a board of management. We are to repudiate the pledges under which they were appointed. We are to remove them from office because we do not like the complexion of their faces or the colour of their hair. Possibly some of them had bee>
associated with those of another politics, stripe. The government is inviting subsequent parliaments, for the same political purposes and with the same view and scope of information, to repudiate the act in order that others who may be more acceptable to a later administration may be appointed in their place. That sort of action is unworthy of parliament. It is impossible for the directors who are to 'be appointed to assume that they are to be above political influence and control. When I say that I refer to political influence and control of a very reprehensibk character, such as we have found in the administration of public bodies in Canada in times past. That is my objection; I can see no sign of improvement in the changes the minister now proposes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Before the section is agreed to there are one or two observations T should like to make. I hope that future parliaments

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
will not get into the habit of changing the set-up of the Canadian National Railways management every time there is a change in the complexion of the House of Commons. It is a dangerous procedure. About 1932 we changed the set-up of the management, and now that there has been a change in government we are to have another change in the management of the Canadian National Railways. Nothing could be more inimical to the management of the railway and the confidence of the people in the Canadian National system than to have a management in which parliament and the people have lost confidence. I believe any government would find it very difficult to obtain the services of the most efficient men to handle the Canadian National Railways if those men thought their positions would be insecure and that they would not be retained if there were a change of government.
The three trustees are in a position where they are asked to resign and to a certain extent their usefulness has been impaired. I cannot see how logically they could remain in office and give the service required of them. But if under the present measure it is intended to appoint a committee of seven to handle the affairs of the railway I suggest that such committee should be appointed by the House of Commons at large rather than by the government. If that were done we would have at least something in the way of permanency of the men in office. I do not know whether the government has considered the suggestion, but I put it to the minister in the hope that it may be helpful. If the leaders of the different parties could get together and decide upon a committee of seven, the men to be appointed would have a greater degree of security than they could have if after a change of government they should find themselves in the position of the present trustees. That is one of the most unfortunate features of the present bill. It dispenses with the services of men, rightly or wrongly, and makes the position insecure. I offer the suggestion to the minister in the hope that he will give it careful consideration and that when a new board of directors is under consideration he will at least consult leaders of other groups in the house, in an effort to appoint a board which will have the full confidence of the House of Commons and the people of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee is dealing with the administration of the most important asset under the control of parliament, namely the Canadian National Railways. It is an asset which represents an enormous investment, an asset which if properly administered and properly developed 12739-215
will make an excellent contribution to the future development of Canada. The people of Canada have invested in this undertaking such an enormous sum of money that anything which relates to its administration should receive the most careful and serious consideration of the House of Commons and of the people of the dominion.
Conditions were such that it was deemed advisable to appoint a royal commission to investigate and consider the administration of the Canadian National Railways. The commission was one that commanded, I think, the confidence of the Canadian people. It undertook the task imposed upon it, and at great length and afteT the expenditure of an enormous sum of money made a report. That report indicated that the method of control or administration of the railways in the past had not been entirely satisfactory, and in pursuance and in keeping with the recommendations of that report a new method of control was devised. It was given the careful consideration of parliament, and that method of control by a board of trustees has been in force now for a little over two years.
The special committee set up to -consider the administration of the Canadian National Railways has just completed its work, and the chairman, of the board of trustees has made to that committee a statement which the minister has commended as a fair, reasonable and moderate one. That statement is not yet available to the members of this house, but it will be printed, I assume, in the votes and proceedings, and I suggest to every member of this committee to read it carefully and seriously. If that is done, then I am of the opinion that the members of this committee will come to the conclusion that the administration of the Canadian National Railways by this board of trustees has been successful; that it has under very difficult and trying conditions accomplished in large measure, so far as the circumstances permitted, the objects which it set out to accomplish; that economies have been made; that improvements in administration have taken place, and that policies have been initiated which, if pursued to their conclusion, will result to the advantage of the railways and of this dominion.
I submit that with that record behind us, with the reasons advanced for a change in the method of administration, and with the fact that we have set up a new organization which has been functioning for so short a time, yet even within which it has been able to demonstrate its value, we ought not now to return to what is to a large extent the form of administration which existed prior to the appointment of this board of trustees. As I under-

C.N.R.-Board of Directors

stand this bill, that is largely what it is; we are in large measure returning to the same old method, control and administration by appointees of the government as we had prior to the investigation by the commission. Results cannot be secured in a short period of time, in the administration of an enormous undertaking like the Canadian National Railways, and I submit that it would be just as sound for a man to plant a tree and in a few months pull it up by the roots to see if it was going to grow as for the minister to make this change at this time. If he will consider the situation he must agree that the board of trustees has not given a sufficient length of time in the control and administration of this road to demonstrate whether the present method is more successful than the old except in so far as the results already indicate that some progress has been made, and I submit that they should have an opportunity _ to demonstrate over a sufficient period of time their capacity to administer the affairs of the road.
The minister in introducing the bill gave some reasons why these changes should be made. I think the reasons he gave have been answered to a large extent by the statement of the chairman of the board of trustees. I submit that the proposed action of the minister under this bill is not in the public interest; that the board of trustees has not been given a sufficient opportunity, and that these changes are not in the interests of the Canadian National Railways or of the people of the Dominion of Canada. If there is one thing that is required it is a continuity of policy, and a change in the method of administration having been made as a result of an investigation by the commission, we ought to have an ample opportunity to test it out to see if it will produce the results which it was hoped it would, especially as there are already indications that good results have followed upon this change in the method of administration.
I submit, finally, that this whole proposition of the minister is a retrograde step; that we are going back to a condition of affairs which was condemned, which was not in the interests of the Canadian National or of its employees or of the people of this dominion, and I fear that the results will be disappointing both to the minister and to the people of Canada as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
In reply, Mr. Chairman, I think we are all agreed that the Duff report made some very sound recommendations, but

whether in appointing the board of trustees the recommendations of the Duff report were followed as exactly as will be the case in the appointment of the seven directors proposed by this bill is a matter for argument. True, the set-up of the board of trustees was the set-up proposed by the Duff commission, but the personnel, as I stated in my opening remarks, hardly followed the recommendations of that report. This type of management was a very unusual one for a commercial corporation as far-flung as the national railways, and under this bill we are going back to the usual business organization. The entire set-up as proposed under this bill is usual in railways, directors being appointed for a three year term, one-third retiring annually, and with a chairman at the head who is an experienced railway man. I think this is the proper time to make the change. At the end of this year one of the trustees retires. I might say that the trustees themselves are quite emphatic in stating that the present system is not a proper one, and that the veto power given the chairman is not a proper power for federal trustees. If we wanted to replace a trustee whose term was up, I do not know where we could find a man of the calibre and background of experience necessary to fill the position. I doubt whether we could fill the position satisfactorily and I think this is the proper time to do what we are doing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Does the minister think a board of seven directors will be more likely than three trustees to carry out the recommendations of the Duff commission? What particular advantage would such a board have over the three trustees? The minister says that some of the provisions of the act are unsatisfactory, but is not the answer to that, amend the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
You have got rid of the old roof; that is my chief objection. The Prime Minister is in the chamber and I should like to have his attention for a moment. The government is now purporting by this bill to repeal some very important provisions of an act passed in 1933 known as the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933. Section 7 of that act, which is now being repealed, reads:
No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
There may be differences of opinion with regard to a pledge contained in a statute passed by the House of Commons and Senate of Canada; there may be differences of opinion with regard to the terms of such pledge when it was under consideration when passing both houses of parliament; but I ask the Prime Minister, even although differences of opinion prevailed at the session of 1933 when the act was passed, is not some consideration to be given to the terms of a pledge which parliament made? Provisions were being made for the appointment of *three trustees to very high and important positions. Those appointments were similar to appointments to a court of appeal or a court of justice where the term was expressed in clear language, with the further provision that no one should be removed from office or suffer a reduction in salary, during the term for which he was appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada. If that provision is to be wiped out by this bill, what confidence can hereafter be placed in the honour and integrity of a parliament that makes such a pledge and then two or three years later repudiates it by allowing the trustees to be removed without assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada after full consideration of the merits or demerits of the charges made against them? That was not a party pledge; it was a pledge contained in a statute passed by a majority of both houses. It declared that the men who were appointed and whose term of office was fixed should not be removed from office except for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada. Such removal as is contemplated by this bill is not in accordance with the pledge.

While I dislike to use strong terms, I think opprobrium, if not dishonour, is placed upon the parliament that refuses to carry out a pledge so made.

Mr. Chairman, may I say to my hon. friend that if at the time that particular clause was inserted there had not been very strong exception taken to it by the then Liberal opposition, I would say he was entirely right in what he is now saying. But one has to consider not only the opposition which was made at the time, but the grounds for it and the nature of it. It was stated very clearly, by the then Liberal opposition, that the particular plan adopted, of having these gentlemen removable only by address of both houses was a Conservative or Tory device to tie the hands of a Liberal administration should we come into office at any future time. I think it was stated very plainly that if that clause did carry, every effort would be made to see that the House of Commons, which was the representative of the people as a whole, would not have its hands tied with respect to the control of any industrial activity for which it might be held responsible.
My hon. friend speaks about the courts of the land and the tenure of office of judges and the grounds on which they are appointed, but this presents no parallel. A judicial position is an entirely different position to that of a director of a company. When a government is held responsible for the success or failure of a great industrial enterprise, it surely should have the right to have as directors of that enterprise persons in whom it has confidence. Otherwise, we would not have responsible government in a true sense.
I wish to repeat that the linking up of the Senate with the House of Commons in the control of everything which relates fundamentally to the finances of the country is a wrong principle and has always been recognized as such. My hon. friend may argue that the Senate was made a party to any dismissal of these gentlemen in order that their tenure of office might be secured, but he overlooks the fact that the House of Commons is the one body responsible for the administration of the different departments of government, that the government of the day has to take responsibility, and that any government returned by the people should, with respect to matters which relate to the finances of the country, be free to deal with those finances as its members think best.
For this reason I believe there is every justification for this particular clause being removed from the act. There is no ground

for contending that this implies any breach of faith or trust on the part of the present administration. As I said, it was made perfectly plain, when we were in opposition, that if we could possibly avoid it we did not propose to have our own and future parliaments bound in a manner which would hold them responsible for the administration, of public affairs and yet deny them the right of having in charge of those affairs persons in whom they had confidence.

That is the only inference, that each successive government will be free to do what it pleases with regard to the provision for the organization and administration of that board, and a new government coming in, which does not like the colour of hair of these directors, or the colour of their eyes, or the particular smile which they bear upon their faces, is at liberty to put them out of office forthwith. Therefore no future tenure of office of directors or trustees of the Canadian National Railways can be regarded as secure. When that principle is once admitted and when parliament, in repudiation of its previous pledges, is prepared to carry out such a policy as that, does it not clearly mean and indicate that the administration of these great railways is to become purely a matter of party politics; that the door is wide open to the return of the system of corruption which we have had in times past in dealing with government railways? That is the precedent which, it seems to me, the right hon. gentleman is establishing. I am discussing this matter apart from his personality; I am not casting reflections upon him. But I do say this, that I do not know of a man in his government -and he has in i/t many members far whom I have high personal respect-there is not one of them, not even himself, who if placed in the position of Minister of Railways in charge of this can be expected to stand between his political party, demanding office

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The principle
I am laying down is that there is no minority which is superior to the majority when that majority is the people of the country as a whole; and the people of the country as a -whole have sent this present House of Commons to legislate with respect to the Canadian National Railways as it thinks right and proper. The whole question of a new enactment with respect to the Canadian National Railways was presented to the people in the last general election. It was one of the policies on which the Liberal opposition took a very strong and positive stand, and it was returned to power in virtue of it and the other policies it outlined. The authority of the present administration in this matter is an authority which has been derived from the people of Canada as a whole, and in no unmistaken voice or way; and we intend to exercise that authority in the light of the responsibility so placed upon us. I wish to take very strong exception to the assumption that just because a director is to be appointed by a Liberal administration he will be thoroughly corrupt in the carrying out of his obligations, whereas a trustee appointed by a Tory administration is always to be above criticism. That is a new doctrine, a principle that does not apply. The only principle that can govern in these matters of the administration of public affairs is the principle of ministerial responsibility. The ministry will be responsible for those whom they appoint as directors. If a mistake is made in the appointment, or if mistakes are made by their appointees, the members of the ministry will be answerable to their masters. But their masters will not be the Tory party but the people of Canada as a whole. That is the essence of the situation. No one knows better than my hon. friend, unless it is his leader, that in most of the legislation which was introduced having to do with financial matters, an effort was made by the previous administration to tie the hands

Questions
of an incoming administration, to tie future parliaments in such a way that they would be bound, not to policies to which they were committed, but to Tory policies which they believed to be inimical to the country's interests. This is one case in point, and it is not by any means the only one. Certainly, however, so far as the present administration is concerned, it is prepared, in so far as it is able, to secure the necessary power and authority to take full responsibility for the legislation it proposes. It is not going to be tied, with respect to what it deems to be necessary and in the public interest, by any clause in any act or agreement which says that with respect to great transactions involving the finances of this country-and that is what is always put up in connection with the Canadian National Railways, that it is a big financial problem

this House of Commons is to be controlled by the other house of parliament. It will in so far as that is possible be controlled solely by its own members, in the exercise of full ministerial responsibility.
